tribe: Banu Salama of al-Khazraj — Ansar of Madina
teaser: He asked Allah to give his household their full share of the plague. Then he buried his sons and his wives.

layers.title: Who
layers.subtitle: The handsomest man in Madina, and the most indebted
layers.content:
Mu'adh ibn Jabal ibn 'Amr, of the Banu Salama of al-Khazraj. His mother was Hind bint Sahl of Juhayna. His kunya was Abu 'Abd ar-Rahman.

Jabir ibn 'Abdullah described him in one line: the handsomest of people in face, the handsomest in physique, and the most generous. Those who sat with him remembered a tall, fair man with a gap between his front teeth, wide eyes, joined eyebrows and very curly hair, with kohl on his eyes and a bright smile.

The third quality cost him. He gave until he was in debt, and then gave more, and his creditors began to press him. There was nothing careless in his religion — he said of himself, 'I have not spat to my right side since I became Muslim' — but with money he was reckless in the direction of other people.

He was also lame in one foot. And he was quiet. Abu Muslim al-Khawlani walked into the mosque at Homs, found some thirty Companions of the Prophet ﷺ sitting there, and noticed one young man who said nothing at all. When the others were unsure of a matter, they got up and went to him.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — description narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah and from the family of Ka'b ibn Malik; Abu Muslim al-Khawlani's account narrated through 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: He went home and broke his clan's idols
layers.content:
He was among the seventy Ansar who gave the pledge at 'Aqaba. Ibn Sa'd notes there is no disagreement in the sources about that.

What he did next tells you the shape of the man. He did not wait for instructions from Makka and he did not keep his Islam quiet. Together with Tha'laba ibn 'Anama and 'Abdullah ibn Unays he went through the Banu Salama and broke their idols — his own clan, his own street, the gods his relatives had grown up feeding.

There is a particular kind of courage in that which has nothing to do with battle. Anyone can be brave among strangers. He made himself unmistakable to the people who would still be at his table the next evening.

The Prophet ﷺ paired him in brotherhood with 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn Sa'd again records no disagreement about it, though Ibn Ishaq alone names Ja'far ibn Abi Talib instead — a report al-Waqidi rejects on grounds of dates, since Ja'far was still in Abyssinia when the pairings were made.

He was twenty or twenty-one at Badr. He was at Uhud, at the Ditch, and at every battle with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — 'Aqaba, the breaking of the idols of Banu Salama, and Muhammad ibn 'Umar's discussion of the brotherhood reports

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: 'By Allah, I love you'
layers.content:
The Prophet ﷺ took him by the hand and told him: 'By Allah, I love you.' Then he gave him something to carry: never leave off saying after every prayer, «اللَّهُمَّ أَعِنِّي عَلَى ذِكْرِكَ وَشُكْرِكَ وَحُسْنِ عِبَادَتِكَ» — O Allah, help me to remember You, to thank You, and to worship You well. Love, and then a task. The two arrived together.

He was sent to Yemen to teach. Before he went the Prophet ﷺ tested him: 'On what will you base your judgement?' 'By what is in the Book of Allah.' 'And if it is not in the Book of Allah?' 'Then by what the Messenger judged.' 'And if it is not in that?' 'I will use my discretion and not neglect.' The Prophet ﷺ struck his chest and praised Allah, who had made his messenger's answer agree with what pleased him. He wrote ahead to the Yemenis: 'I have sent you one of the best of my people to take charge of your knowledge and your deen.'

And of him the Prophet ﷺ said: 'The one of my community with the best knowledge of the lawful and the unlawful is Mu'adh ibn Jabal.'

Mu'adh remembered the last thing said to him as his foot went into the stirrup. Not a ruling. Have good character with people.
layers.hadith_ref: Sunan Abu Dawud, Book of the Prayer, narrated by Mu'adh ibn Jabal — 'By Allah, I love you' and the du'a after every prayer
layers.source: Sunan Abu Dawud, Book of the Prayer; the Yemen dialogue narrated from al-Harith ibn 'Amr ath-Thaqafi, the letter from Ibn Abi Najih, the stirrup advice from Yahya ibn Sa'id, and the praise from Anas ibn Malik — all in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III

layers.title: The Trial and Quality
layers.subtitle: Stripped to nothing, and he would not ask
layers.content:
His creditors ran out of patience. For some days he stayed inside his house rather than face them, and they went over his head to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: take what we are owed out of him.

He was summoned and came with them. The Prophet ﷺ first tried mercy — 'May Allah have mercy on whoever gives him charity' — and some gave, and some stood there and repeated their demand. So his property was taken from him and divided among them, and it covered five-sevenths of the debt. Still not satisfied, they said: then sell him to us. The Prophet ﷺ closed it: 'Leave him. You have no way against him.'

Mu'adh walked back to the Banu Salama with nothing. Someone said to him, Abu 'Abd ar-Rahman, you are destitute now, go and ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said: 'I will not ask him.'

A day later he was called and sent to Yemen. 'Perhaps Allah will mend him and settle his debts.'

And when Yemen did make him wealthy, he was frightened of it. Meeting 'Umar at Mina, he was told to hand his gifted servants to Abu Bakr and refused sharply. That night he dreamt he was at the lip of a fire with 'Umar holding his waist. He woke, went to Abu Bakr, and handed them over.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah through Mu'adh ibn Rifa'a, and the Mina account narrated from Shaqiq through al-A'mash

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: 'You choke me, and You know I love You'
layers.content:
The plague of 'Amwas reached Syria while he was there. When Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah fell ill he put Mu'adh in charge, and the people came to Mu'adh saying, pray to Allah to take this filth away from us.

He would not let them call it that. 'Do you make a mercy that Allah has bestowed on His slaves like a punishment He inflicted on a people He was angry with? It is a mercy singled out for you, and a martyrdom singled out for you.' Then, out loud, in front of them: 'O Allah, give the family of Mu'adh their full portion of this mercy.'

His two sons fell ill. He asked how they were and they answered that the truth was from their Lord and he would find them, Allah willing, among the steadfast. Then his two wives fell ill and died. Then it took him — in his thumb first, and he kept touching it to his mouth and saying, 'O Allah, it is small. Bless it. You bless the small.' It moved to his throat. Al-Harith ibn 'Amira sat with him and heard him fainting and reviving and saying: 'Choke me. By Your might, I love You.'

He died in 18 AH under 'Umar. Reports differ on his age — one account says thirty-eight, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said thirty-three. No line survived him. 'Umar used to say that if he ever met Mu'adh he would appoint him, and answer for it before Allah with what he had heard the Prophet ﷺ say: when the scholars are gathered on the Day of Rising, Mu'adh ibn Jabal will be a stone's throw ahead of them.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — the 'Amwas account narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Rafi' and from Dawud ibn al-Husayn; the deathbed words from al-Harith ibn 'Amira az-Zubaydi and from Salama ibn Kuhayl; 'Umar's words narrated from Shahr ibn Hawshab

quiz.prompt: What did Mu'adh do among his own clan, the Banu Salama, immediately after becoming Muslim?

options.text: He led them in the first congregational prayer in Madina
He broke their idols, along with two other men
He kept his Islam secret for a year
He gave away his father's inheritance

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Tha'laba ibn 'Anama and 'Abdullah ibn Unays were with him. Three young men dismantling the shrines of their own relatives, who were not going anywhere.

quiz.prompt: When the Prophet ﷺ asked how he would judge in Yemen if a matter was in neither the Book nor the Sunnah, what did Mu'adh answer?

options.text: 'I will write to you and wait'
'I will ask the elders of Yemen'
'I will use my discretion and not neglect'
'I will refuse to judge'

quiz.citation: Narrated from al-Harith ibn 'Amr ath-Thaqafi — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ struck his chest and praised Allah for making the answer agree with what pleased him. The whole later science of legal reasoning rests on that short exchange.

quiz.prompt: What happened to Mu'adh's property when his creditors pressed the Prophet ﷺ for payment?

options.text: The Prophet ﷺ paid the debt from the treasury
It was taken and divided among them, covering five-sevenths of the debt
The creditors forgave the whole amount
He was ordered to sell his house in Yemen

quiz.citation: Narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: They then asked to have him sold to recover the rest. The Prophet ﷺ answered, 'Leave him. You have no way against him.' Destitution was permitted. Ownership of a Muslim's person was not.

quiz.prompt: How did Mu'adh answer the people of Syria when they called the plague of 'Amwas a filth?

options.text: He agreed and led them in prayer for it to be lifted
He told them to leave the region immediately
He called it a mercy and a martyrdom, and asked Allah to give his own household their full share of it
He said it was a punishment for their sins

quiz.citation: Narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Rafi' and from Dawud ibn al-Husayn — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was not speaking about other people's households when he said it. His two sons, then his two wives, then he himself all died of it.

quiz.prompt: What did al-Harith ibn 'Amira hear Mu'adh say as he was dying of the plague in his throat?

options.text: 'Bury me in Madina'
'Choke me. By Your might, I love You'
'Tell 'Umar I forgive him'
'I have left no debt behind me'

quiz.citation: Narrated from al-Harith ibn 'Amira az-Zubaydi through Shahr ibn Hawshab — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Another chain records it as, 'O Lord, You choke me, and You know I love You.' He did not ask for the choking to stop. He named who was doing it and said what he thought of Him.

quiz.prompt: The Prophet ﷺ said 'I love you' to Mu'adh and immediately gave him a du'a to keep. How do you tend to receive affection that comes with a responsibility attached?

options.text: I take the affection and quietly drop the responsibility
The responsibility is how I know the affection was real
I find it hard to believe I am loved unless I am useful
I have never separated the two and cannot imagine doing so

quiz.citation: Reflection on Sunan Abu Dawud, Book of the Prayer, narrated by Mu'adh ibn Jabal
quiz.scholar_reflection: The du'a asks for help with three things: remembering Him, thanking Him, worshipping Him well. It assumes all three are beyond us without assistance.

quiz.prompt: He was destitute and told to go and ask, and he said, 'I will not ask him.' Where is your line on asking for help?

options.text: I ask too late, and it costs other people as well as me
I ask easily and I have stopped feeling bad about it
I will ask for others but not for myself
I would rather be in real difficulty than owe someone a favour

quiz.citation: Narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not ask, and he was still sent for the next day. Note who initiated it. Restraint is not the same as being left alone.

quiz.prompt: Mu'adh refused 'Umar's instruction about the servants, then a dream changed his mind overnight. What actually shifts you when you have dug in?

options.text: Fear — I move when I see the consequence
A person I trust saying it a second time, gently
Nothing quickly; I need time alone with it
Honestly, being embarrassed in front of someone

quiz.citation: Narrated from Shaqiq through al-A'mash — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had said, am I given something and then told to hand it over. By morning he said, I only think that I should obey you. He reversed himself out loud, to the man he had refused.

quiz.prompt: In a mosque full of senior Companions, Mu'adh sat silent and they came to him. What is your relationship with silence in a room where you know something?

options.text: I speak first and reconsider afterwards
I stay quiet out of caution and sometimes regret it
I stay quiet because I want to be asked
It depends entirely on who else is in the room

quiz.citation: Narrated from Abu Muslim al-Khawlani — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Two separate men, in two separate cities, walked into a mosque and noticed the same thing: the young one was not talking, and everyone else deferred to him.

quiz.prompt: Dying, he prayed over his infected thumb: 'O Allah, it is small. Bless it. You bless the small.' How do you handle the small pains, as opposed to the large ones?

options.text: I only pray about the large ones and feel silly otherwise
The small ones wear me down far more than the large ones
I complain about the small and stay silent about the large
I have learned to bring everything, without ranking it

quiz.citation: Narrated from Dawud ibn al-Husayn and 'Abdullah ibn Rafi' — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had buried two sons and two wives that month. The thing he made du'a over was his thumb, and he made a theological point out of its smallness.
